topic: The Pi Machine: How Colliding Blocks Compute the Digits of Pi
target_audience: Advanced high school students and undergraduate physics/math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: A Strange Counting Game
lecture_lines: Imagine two blocks on a frictionless surface.
A small mass m and a large mass M.
We count every collision with the wall or each other.
animations: Draw #FFFFFF floor and [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/wall.svg]; place #00FF00 [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] 'm' and #0000FF [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] 'M'.
Animate #0000FF [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] 'M' moving left, colliding with 'm'.
Show 'm' bouncing off [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/wall.svg]; increment #FF00FF 'Clacks' counter to 2.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of the 'Clack'
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions follow two fundamental laws of physics.
Momentum and energy are conserved in every impact.
No energy is lost as heat during these collisions.
animations: Display conservation equations for momentum and energy in #FFFFFF.
Highlight the energy equation with a #FFFF00 pulse.
Draw v and V axes; plot a #00FFFF ellipse representing energy.

sections.title: The Patterns Emerge
lecture_lines: For equal masses, we count three total collisions.
Increase the large mass by a factor of 100.
Now we count thirty-one collisions between the blocks.
Larger mass ratios reveal the digits of Pi.
The collision count mirrors three point one four one.
animations: M=1: Animate 3 collisions; update #FF00FF counter.
M=100: Animate 31 collisions with faster 'clack' sounds.
M=10000: Rapidly count to 314 collisions on screen.
Highlight the resulting numbers 3, 31, 314 in #FFFF00.
Fade in #FFFFFF symbol for Pi next to the counter.

sections.title: Mapping Physics to Geometry (Phase Space)
lecture_lines: Scale the velocities to transform physics into geometry.
The conservation of energy now forms a perfect circle.
Each collision jumps to a new point on the circle.
Every impact represents a fixed angle of rotation.
Physics becomes a journey around a circular path.
animations: Display the velocity ellipse from the previous section.
Scale the V-axis by sqrt(M/m), transforming ellipse to #00FFFF circle.
Mark the initial state as a #FFFFFF point on the circle.
Animate a #FF0000 chord representing the first collision's velocity change.
Animate successive chords jumping around the circle's circumference.

sections.title: The Final Reveal: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: The mass ratio determines the angle of each jump.
Heavier masses result in much smaller angular steps.
Total collisions represent a trip halfway around the circle.
We divide Pi radians by this tiny collision angle.
This explains why the digits of Pi emerge.
animations: Zoom into the circle to show the angle theta between points.
Label the angle as arctan(sqrt(m/M)) in #00FF00, using [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/mass.svg] to represent the mass parameters.
Show the total arc of the semicircle representing pi radians.
Animate the path of chords filling the pi-radian arc.
Display 'Total collisions = Pi / theta' in #FFFF00.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Unity of Math and Nature
lecture_lines: Colliding blocks act as a mechanical computer for Pi.
Geometry is deeply embedded in the laws of motion.
Simple physics reveals the most fundamental mathematical constants.
animations: Animate both blocks [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/blocks.svg] sliding to the right, away from the wall.
Display '3.14159...' in large #FFFFFF font at center.
Fade all elements to black, leaving a glowing Pi symbol.
